trans.sense: comrade, especially with reference to the former USSR — see also comrade

examples.text: Instead of addressing them according to revolutionary etiquette as Tovarish (comrade), he asked them their Christian names and that of their fathers, while telling them his own.
examples.ref: 1919 December 6, The Times, p.10 col. C:

examples.text: Touching one of them on the shoulder, she said, “Tovarish, these tovarishes want to know who you are.”
examples.ref: 1938, Margaret Sanger, Margaret Sanger: An Autobiography:

examples.text: Jensen laughed, “My wife complains: ‘All day long they ring our door bell. Tovarish here, tovarish there. They come from Moscow, from Leningrad, from Berlin and Hamburg. They don't speak one word of Danish. Comrade Jensen, they say, fix us up with Danish passports.’ So it goes.″
examples.ref: 1940, Jan Valtin, Out of the Night, Kessinger Publishing Company, published 2005, page 436:

examples.text: His Russian was derived from a fortnight's crash course. "You'd better see what this ah tovarish thinks he wants."
examples.ref: 1989, Anthony Burgess, “Pedwar”, in Any Old Iron, London: Hutchinson, →ISBN; republished New York, N.Y.: Washington Square Press, Pocket Books, 1990, →ISBN, page 173:

examples.text: The tovarishes bring along their harmonicas and balalaikas, their good voices and their good humor.
